messages.content: Write an internal post arguing for blameless postmortems at a company that does not do them yet. Around 250 words.

**We keep asking the wrong first question**

July's checkout outage ran four hours. The actual fix took about twenty minutes. Everything else was people deciding how much of what they knew was safe to say out loud.

None of that shows up in the incident report. When the first question in the room is "whose deploy was it," everybody starts editing. The engineer who spotted the config drift a couple of weeks earlier and never wrote it down says nothing. The one who approved a PR at six on a Friday spends the meeting defending the PR. Nobody lies. We just end up with the version that's cheapest to admit to, and then we write our action items against that version.

Blameless postmortems are not a courtesy we extend to each other. They're a method for getting a true account, which is a thing we currently do not have. Start from the assumption that everyone did something sensible with the information in front of them at the time. If the answer looks obvious afterwards, the interesting question is what our tooling failed to show.

Three changes. Build the timeline first, and let nobody propose an action until it's finished. Keep names out of the write-up, roles only. Get someone who wasn't on the rotation to run the meeting, because you cannot chair a room and be candid in it at the same time.

Accountability survives all of this. It just means owning the repair instead of wearing the fault. Today we get the fault and pay in outages we never actually understood.

I'll facilitate the next one this way if people are willing.
Rewrite the text above. Keep the same length and the same purpose. Return only the rewritten text.

output:
**Our first question is the wrong one**

The checkout outage in July lasted four hours. Fixing it took twenty minutes. The rest was people working out how much of what they knew could safely be said in the room.

None of that made the incident report. When the meeting opens with "whose deploy was it," everyone starts editing. The engineer who noticed the config drift two weeks earlier and never filed anything keeps quiet. The one who approved a PR at six on a Friday spends the hour defending the PR. Nobody lies. We just get the version that's cheapest to admit to, and then we write our action items against it.

Blameless postmortems aren't a kindness we do for each other. They're a way of getting a true account, which is something we don't currently have. Assume everyone did something sensible with what they could see at the time. If a decision looks obvious in hindsight, the question worth asking is what our tooling failed to show.

Three changes. Build the timeline first, and let nobody propose an action until it's finished. Names out of the write-up, roles only. Have someone off the rotation run the meeting, since you can't chair a room and speak candidly in it at the same time.

Accountability doesn't go anywhere. It shifts to owning the repair instead of wearing the fault. Right now we get the fault, and we pay for it in outages we never understood.

I'll facilitate the next one this way if people are up for it.
